habitat.description: Staghorn corals are foundational reef-building species found in shallow tropical waters, typically between 1 and 30 meters depth. They form dense thickets that provide critical three-dimensional structure for thousands of other marine species. Requiring clear, warm water (23-29 degrees Celsius) with abundant light, they are among the most sensitive corals to environmental change.

threats.name: Ocean Warming
threats.description: Even 1-2 degrees Celsius above normal triggers mass bleaching events where corals expel symbiotic algae and starve. Back-to-back bleaching prevents recovery.

threats.name: Ocean Acidification
threats.description: Absorbed CO2 makes seawater more acidic, dissolving calcium carbonate skeletons faster than corals can build them.

threats.name: Disease
threats.description: White band disease and stony coral tissue loss disease have devastated staghorn populations, killing entire reef systems within months.

threats.name: Coastal Pollution
threats.description: Nutrient runoff from agriculture fuels algal blooms that smother corals, while sediment blocks the light they need to survive.

conservationStatus.population: Population has declined by over 80% since the 1980s across the Caribbean
keyPrograms: Assisted gene flow and selective breeding

culturalSignificance.overview: Coral reefs are often called the 'rainforests of the sea,' supporting 25% of all marine species while covering less than 1% of the ocean floor. They protect coastlines, support fisheries feeding hundreds of millions of people, and generate billions in tourism revenue. Their decline represents one of the most visible consequences of climate change.
literature: Coral Reefs in the Microbial Seas by Forest Rohwer
culturalSignificance.symbolism: Represents biodiversity, ecological interconnection, and climate vulnerability. The coral reef is a living barometer of ocean health and a warning system for planetary change.
